content.thinking:
Now I'm settling on the design: a treasure hoard prop group in League of Legends style—exaggerated dynamic shapes, high-contrast saturated accents, glowing magic details, readable from a top-down camera. Most objects stay plain, but the chest lid needs a hinge joint, so I'm considering whether a root joint is required even though the guide allows plain objects for most props.

I'll create a root joint at origin with a separate hinge joint for the lid, keeping everything else parented to the root to stay safe. For the scene itself, I'm sketching a roughly 1.6m x 1.6m hoard: a mound of scattered coins, an open chest with an ornate hinged lid spilling coins and gems, a crown resting on the mound, a few goblets (some standing, one tipped), glowing gem clusters, and small extras like a necklace or ring to round things out—while keeping a scattered coin patch on the ground instead of a full base.

Now I'm sizing things out: chest roughly 0.9m wide, coin mound about 1.3m wide and 0.6m tall, crown ~0.3m, goblets ~0.25m tall, with the chest positioned at back center and coins spilling forward plus side piles, crown and goblets arranged across the heap. I'm starting to build the coins as cylinder geometries grouped by color for merging.

Designing coin texture...

Checking triangle budgets, I figure merging the circle face geometry with the cylinder works since both share uv/normal/position attributes. Dropping to 8 radial segments keeps each coin around 40 triangles, so 600 coins stays near 24k triangles, comfortably under the 60k budget.

I'm now thinking I can skip the cylinder caps entirely since bottoms stay hidden in the pile, and just texture the top face with a decal circle offset slightly above the coin surface. To keep draw calls low I'll use one greyscale emboss texture tinted per coin type -- gold using a warm hex tone and silver using a cool pale blue tint -- rather than generating separate full-color textures.

For the mound itself I'm figuring out how to scatter coin positions across a heap surface defined by a gaussian-like height falloff, tilting each coin toward the local slope plus some randomness, with a solid dark-gold ellipsoid body underneath to fill the base so gaps aren't visible through the coin layer.

Then I'm sizing the coins at roughly 4-5.5cm radius and estimating I'll need around 600-700 of them to cover a mound footprint of about 0.4 square meters with enough overlap for a natural piled look, keeping the triangle budget manageable around 24k.

For heap placement, I want several distinct piles: a main heap spilling left out of the chest, a front heap sloping down toward the viewer, a smaller right heap topped with goblets, and a left heap crowned with... something regal. I'm modeling each heap as a sum of gaussian bumps centered at different points, and now I need to figure out how coins fill the chest's hollow interior so it looks full right up to the rim when viewed through the opening.

I'm building the chest as an open box shell with separate floor and wall slabs, then filling the interior with a mounded coin heap rising slightly above the rim. For coin placement, I'm sampling candidate positions and computing heights from the heap function, while skipping points that fall inside wall thickness zones and capping interior coin height near the rim so it reads as an overflowing mound.

Now I'm defining the chest's actual dimensions—roughly 0.95 wide by 0.6 deep, 0.42 tall, centered toward the back of the scene—with the lid hinge placed along the far edge so the open rim sits at that top height.

For the lid itself, I'm thinking of it as a barrel-vaulted shape, like a half-cylinder, built as an extruded arch profile with thickness running along the horizontal axis and curved iron strap details across the planks. Since the lid swings open to roughly 110°, the viewer would actually be looking at its underside/interior face from this angle.

So I'll add a dark wood inner surface with a red velvet lining panel and gold trim rather than modeling a hollow shell, since the solid half-disc extrusion already reads correctly as the flat interior face when the lid is open. I'm placing the hinge joint along the back edge on the X-axis so the lid rotates open from that pivot point.

I'm working out the rotation math to make the lid tip up and backward correctly, calculating that a -110° rotation about the X-axis sends the forward-pointing direction up and back as needed for the open pose.

Since anything built after a joint's pose lands in that new orientation, I need to build the lid parts first while the joint is still closed, then apply the 110° pose afterward so the geometry rotates together correctly. I'm also checking that the lid's extent, once tilted back at that angle, doesn't overshoot the box's footprint.

For the palette, I'm going for a League of Legends feel — saturated gold tones (lit, mid, shadow shades) with painterly rather than toon-style contrast, and reserving the glowing kit effect for gems and coins to make them pop.

I'm keeping the painted texture area limited to the chest, crown, goblets, and base heap, while coins stay flat-colored cylinders to save texel budget, and I'm planning a strong accent color scheme—hextech cyan-teal glow contrasting with warm gold, plus mixed gem colors like ruby red for visual variety.

Now I'm defining the specific gem palette: ruby, emerald, sapphire, amethyst, and a cyan glow tone for the magical hextech heart jewel embedded in the crown and chest lock. I'm thinking through how emissive strength should be tuned low enough that facet shading still reads, rather than flattening everything into a single glowing color at full strength.

I'm working out the lathe geometry for cut gems—using a low-segment profile with table, crown, girdle, and pavilion points so the facets stay flat-shaded and gem-like rather than smooth.

I need to merge gem geometries using THREE.LatheGeometry directly rather than relying on the builder's part wrapper, making sure all meshes use consistent indexed/non-indexed attributes so the merge doesn't break.

For the gems' glow effect, I'm thinking through how flat colors per gem material will interact with per-color glow copies, then considering sparkle accents on top — maybe card-based sparkle flares oriented toward the camera, figuring out how frame facing direction should work for cards that stand upright versus lean toward the viewer.

For the sparkles, I'm settling on using cross-cards (two perpendicular quads) so they read from any viewing angle, plus adding a flat horizontal card to avoid the edge-on problem from a top-down view — roughly 14 sparkles total, glowing and sharing a texture atlas. I'm also considering whether to add a cyan hextech-style glowing crystal cluster behind the chest as a bigger magical centerpiece.

Then I decide to anchor the hoard scene with a low octagonal stone dais (about 2.2m across, 0.06m high) topped with a glowing cyan rune ring to improve top-down readability without overscoping the piece, using a lathe-based octagon with dark violet-grey cobbled texturing.

Now I'm working out the overall dimensions concretely — placing the rune ring just above the dais surface with coins scattered on top, estimating overall height from the open lid and crystal cluster (roughly up to 1 meter tall), and pinning down the chest's exact position, width, depth, and body height in world coordinates.

Building the chest geometry...

Writing extrude and grain paint logic...

For the open lid at 110°, the underside shown from the front needs a red velvet lining with gold trim, so I'm planning a quilted diamond-pattern textured plane inset within the flat rectangular face, oriented downward in the closed pose.

I also need to handle the chest interior visible with coins when opened, plus curved metal straps running along the lid's arch outline, offset slightly outward near the sides.

Still working out the arc parameterization...

Now I'm setting up the lid's hinge joint at the back edge, aiming it forward so I can later rotate it open by about 108 degrees once the closed-pose geometry is complete.

I'm also designing a hasp lock mechanism — a gold plate with a keyhole on the lid that separates from a glowing cyan gem lock plate on the chest body when the lid opens. Then I'm working out a height function to shape coin mounds piling inside and around the chest, defining bump positions, sizes, and amplitudes relative to the dais and interior floor level.

Adding left and right coin heaps plus a trailing spill toward the front-right, and scattering loose flat coins across the dais floor out to the rim. Since the bump heights sum, overlapping heaps will naturally stack taller, which I'll need to clip appropriately.

For placing individual coins, I'm sampling positions weighted toward the bumps, computing each coin's height on the pile, and orienting it using the surface normal derived from the local gradient blended with some random tilt and spin so the pile looks natural rather than perfectly uniform. I'm working out how to rotate the cylinder geometry from its default axis to align with that normal vector.

I also want to add a base mound mesh beneath the scattered coins so there's no dark gap showing through — a custom heightfield grid slightly below the coin surface, colored dark gold, matching the same non-radial bump shape as the coin distribution.

I need to check that the heightfield doesn't poke through the chest walls where the heap overlaps the chest's box region — since outside-bump heights stay below the rim height there, they should remain hidden inside the solid walls rather than clipping through visibly.

With a 28×24 grid I'm getting 1344 triangles total, which seems reasonable. The coin heaps near the chest sides (x=±0.75) lean against the chest walls with enough amplitude to look natural, while the back of the chest stays clear since heaps only extend to positive z.

Now I'm checking whether the heap field extends beyond the octagonal dais radius — some points reach past the 1.2 circumradius, so I need to mask the coin heightfield to stay within roughly r<1.1 to avoid coins floating off the dais edge.

Rather than letting the heightfield degrade awkwardly outside that boundary, I realize I need the flat portion of the field clamped just below the dais surface so it doesn't poke through the dais wall, and I'm narrowing the grid domain itself to fit within the octagon's apothem rather than its circumradius to avoid corner points sticking outside the platform.

Now I'm sizing up the dais itself — an 8-sided lathe with circumradius 1.35 and apothem 1.25, with the dais top at y=0.07 and bottom resting at y=0 so the object floor sits flush. I'm also setting up coin variety: thin cylinders roughly 0.014 thick, split across gold, lighter gold, and silver tones in a 65/20/15 mix.

Each coin needs a flat-colored rim distinct from its tinted face texture, so I'm defining darker rim colors for gold, light gold, and silver. For efficiency I'm merging coins by type into three cylinder groups and three textured face groups, with small circle geometries rotated to face outward along each coin's axis, and allowing some coins to be randomly flipped upside down so not all faces point the same way on the heap.

Writing SVG emblem code...

Since the coin faces are tiny at this scale, a 128px texture is plenty. For the crown I'm thinking LoL-style exaggeration: a tall spiky shape with curved prongs tipped in gem orbs and a larger cyan gem centered, built from a lathed base band with a flared rim.

I'm sizing it roughly 0.3m across and 0.26m tall with prongs adding another 0.2m, sitting tilted atop the left coin heap. Working out the band's lathe profile for the inner/outer walls and gold paint, then defining five curved prongs sweeping outward from the band top using polar coordinates for their base and mid radii.

Alternating tall and short prongs with gem tips, tube-swept gold shapes, and small spheres for the colored gem orbs at each tip. Adding a large front gem on the band itself.

I'm also layering in a velvet cap inside the crown using a lathed dome profile for the crimson interior, plus a classic ermine fur trim band (white with black spots) at the base to make it instantly recognizable as a royal crown.

For the overall tilt, I'm planning a coordinate-mapping helper that converts crown-local points to world space by rotating and translating, so each piece—lathes, sweeps, and oriented parts—stays consistent when the whole crown is angled.

I'll use the region helper so `C.p()` gives model points and `C.d()` gives rotated axes for the lathe. For the three goblets, I'm planning exaggerated LoL-style designs — flared bowls, thin twisted stems with knobs, and flared bases, starting with a gold one.

Writing lathe profile coordinates...

That axis closure should be fine since degenerate edges there don't matter. Now I'm thinking through the goblet's liquid disc, gold rim band, gem studs around the bowl base, and whether to add an engraved filigree decal on the curved bowl surface.

I'll make the decal face the camera with a simple pattern of diamonds and scrolls in orange/brown and cyan over the gold base. Now I'm placing the two goblets: one upright on the right coin heap, the other tipped over on its side in front of the chest with coins spilling from its mouth.

I'm also adding a taller chalice upright on the left heap, plus neat coin-stack towers of 5-9 coins each near the front-left, computing their resting height from the heap surface and adding a few coins standing on edge for variety.

For gems, I'm picking a palette of ruby, emerald, sapphire, amethyst, and cyan, each with matching glow colors and sizes between 0.04-0.09, scattering roughly 28 lathe-cut gems across the heap with random tilts at heights based on the heap surface.

I'm also adding a couple of hero-sized cut gems (0.14) near the chest front, plus crystal clusters rising from the back corners -- cyan hexagonal crystals on one side and amethyst-pink on the other, using six-segment lathe shapes with flat facets and moderate glow, positioned where the heap height is low so they appear to emerge from the base.

For extra detail I'm planning a pearl necklace draped across the front heap -- a closed catmull-rom curve tracing an irregular loop with small merged pearl spheres along it, plus a gold clasp and pendant gem, and maybe a separate gold ring with its own gem lying on the heap, and possibly a tipped-over coin purse spilling coins for added realism.

I'm also sketching a small drawstring pouch near the left heap with a red tie band, skipping extras like a dagger, candle, or scepter to stay on-theme. For a rune ring on the dais, I'm considering a flat plane texture facing upward with a glowing cyan ring and glyph tick marks, sized for a 512 texture with strokes thick enough to read clearly, though I'm wary coins might end up covering it.

For visibility, I'm placing the ring at an outer radius just beyond the coin heaps so it peeks out, with an outer edge and an inner decorative circle, then setting the dais border apothem accordingly. For the dais rim itself, I'm shaping a beveled lathe profile and rotating the segments so flat faces point forward, working out the circumradius-to-apothem math to keep the geometry aligned, and planning a dark violet stone finish with cobbled detailing.

Now I'm painting the stone surface with a mottled violet-to-indigo color scheme with darker grout lines, adding a darker beveled outer band, and placing small glowing cyan gem studs on gold octagonal posts at the eight corner vertices of the dais for readability and visual interest.

I'm staying under the color budget, defining a gold palette with lit and shadow tones for painted gold parts, then layering in a subtle mottled highlight texture to simulate wear and shine.

For wood, I'm defining grain textures with directional noise for different parts like lathe tubes versus slats, plus a darker wood tone for the lid frame. I'm also planning plank seams on the chest body walls using periodic darkening along vertical position to simulate boards meeting.

For the lid's curved surface, I realize vertical position doesn't map cleanly to seams the way it does on flat walls, so instead I'm working out plank seams along the arc using angular coordinates computed from the extrusion's outline, placing seam lines at regular angle intervals to mimic curved boards following the dome shape.

Now I'm listing the chest's component parts: four chunky corner feet, the body walls with planked wood coloring, and an interior floor panel.

I'm adding more hardware details—bottom and top trim bands in gold, gold L-shaped corner brackets with rivets, vertical metal straps with rivet rows, and a gold lock plate on the front.

For the lock plate itself, I'm extruding a shield-shaped outline with a bevel and setting a glowing cyan gem in the center, skipping the keyhole detail for simplicity. Then I'm thinking through the interior lining—whether red velvet wall panels would even be visible above the coin mound, since the coins likely cover most of the interior walls except possibly near the back rim.

I'm adding thin inset boxes colored like red velvet for the back and side interior panels instead of full lining planes. For the lid, working in closed-pose coordinates relative to the hinge, I'm matching its span to the body but slightly thicker for overhang, adding an underside velvet-textured plane, and placing wood ribs near the arch sweeps at the edges.

Now I'm positioning the gold end trims along the arch outline, deciding on iron-dark strap placements across the lid with a gold-tipped look, leaving a center gap for the hasp, and starting the gold trim strip along the lid's front bottom edge.

I'm now shaping the hasp as a hanging gold plate at the front center that would cover the lock when closed, placing a vertical tab extending down over the body front.

 With body top set at yH=0.47, I position the hasp from y=0.50 down to 0.38, and place a lock shield centered at y=0.30 with the gem embedded in it. Then I check the hinge rotation at the back edge, making sure the lid tips forward correctly when rotated -108° about the X axis.

I'm working through the trigonometry for the open-lid pose: computing the rotated y/z coordinates for the lid's forward edge and arch bulge, which lands the front edge near (1.02, -0.77) and pushes the bulge backward and slightly down. This puts the overall chest height around 1.05m with the lid open, against a roughly 2.7m width, which feels right for a sizeable treasure hoard container with the body itself at 0.47m tall.

Now I'm figuring out the crown's placement, anchoring it on top of the front-left heap peak, and working through the viewer's orientation—since the camera sits at +Z looking toward -Z, I need to pin down whether +X ends up on the viewer's right using a cross product of forward and up vectors.

Defining heap bumps...

I'm repositioning the crystal clusters so they don't overlap the crown—cyan cluster moves to the left-back, amethyst stays right-back, with the crown placed in front at (0.7, 0.05). Now I'm figuring out where to place the goblet.

I'm placing Goblet A with cyan near the left heap, deciding Goblet B should be tipped on its side spilling coins forward toward the viewer in a fanned cone pattern, and setting Goblet C upright and tall with an emerald on the front lump. I'm also considering adding a pearl necklace draped on one of the nearby lumps.

For the smaller treasures, I'm placing a pouch near the edge, a ring near the floor at the dais front, and figuring out where the heightfield for loose coins caps out. I'm now thinking through how coin heaps should interact with other objects -- letting coins embed naturally under goblets and the crystal base, but excluding coins from poking through the crown's hollow interior since its bottom rim should rest cleanly on the coin surface.

For the crown specifically, I'm deciding to exclude coins within a small radius of its center so the rim can sink slightly and hide the gap, with the velvet cap dome covering it from above. For the goblets, I'm working out a similar exclusion radius around the foot so coins don't visibly intersect the base.

For the tipped goblet, I'm scripting a fan of spilled coins pouring from the mouth along an axis toward the camera, mostly lying flat with a few standing upright, blended into the general coin list through a special placement function.

Tallying up the scene's total triangle budget — coins, stacks, spilled coins, floor coins, gems, crystals, chest, and crown — I'm estimating around 40k triangles, comfortably under the 60k limit, though I'm considering trimming coin cylinder caps to save a bit more.

I'm deciding to keep each coin as a simple low-poly cylinder with 8 radial segments, verifying the triangle edges stay fine enough relative to the scene's overall diagonal, and nudging the face decal slightly above the cylinder top to avoid z-fighting at typical camera distance. I'm also weighing whether to build the cylinder without end caps and add separate textured top/bottom circles instead, to keep material tinting distinct between the rim and faces.

For merging, I'm making sure the cylinder and circle geometries share the same attribute layout so they can combine cleanly, applying transforms via matrix multiplication, and using flat shading throughout for a consistent faceted lowpoly look. I'm rotating the face circles to point outward correctly, letting their spin be randomized, and handling texture tinting so grey textures still pick up the fill color while already-colored textures stay as-is.

Now I'm planning the sparkle effects: small four-point star glows in white/cyan, sized around 0.14, placed at roughly 16 key spots like big gems, crown tips, goblet rims, and the hasp. I'm considering adding a magical cyan glow rising from the chest interior using light-shaft style cards, though I'm wary of how the hard-edged alpha-cut rays will read silhouette-wise, going for a "hextech glow" aesthetic.

I'm swapping the risky light rays for a simpler set of six thin sparkle crosses instead, skipping the rays entirely. Now I'm setting up the code structure, importing geometry merge utilities, math/path helpers, paint and texture modules, and the toon/glow kits, then sketching the skeleton with a root "hoard" joint and a hinged lid joint, making sure every part call is bound to the correct nearest joint so nothing attaches to the wrong bone.

To avoid that bone-mismatch bug, I'm writing small wrapper functions that default non-lid parts to the root bone and lid parts to the lid bone, plus a basic box-adding helper and a seeded random generator. Now I'm defining the bump data and chest dimensions, then building helper functions to check whether a point falls inside the chest's interior or outer box, and starting a heap-height function that uses those interior checks to shape the gold pile.

Now I'm refining the heap-height function: inside the chest, the floor dips and rises into a dome so coins overflow slightly above the rim height, while a bump-and-fade calculation shapes the mound elsewhere. I'm checking the math so the dome peaks around 0.49 at center but still sits near the rim height of 0.40 at the edges, giving a believable overflowing coin pile, and verifying that regions outside the interior but within the chest walls stay low enough to not clip through the walls.

I also need to handle coin rejection near wall zones, compute surface gradients via finite differences for coin orientation, add some randomized tilt so coins don't look perfectly aligned, and vary vertical placement slightly so coins appear naturally layered rather than floating or buried. I'm also thinking through how to sample bump centers using a Gaussian distribution weighted by area and amplitude, and whether to filter out overly thin piles so coins don't poke through flat ground.

For the interior chest coins, I'm setting up a separate sampling loop confined to the inner box so pieces don't clip through the walls, adjusting the usable range to account for coin radius. I'm reusing the heap-point sampler for gem placement too, defining coin size and thickness ranges, and splitting coin colors into gold, a secondary gold variant, and silver by probability. Now I'm writing the lathe-based gem geometry function...

Still defining crystal geometry...

I'll skip the lighter-core idea for now and move to the chest pieces, writing small helper functions and iterating with preview shots since renders are limited but previews aren't. I need to check the region.ts source to confirm the signature for region placement and joint options before wiring up the crown.

I'm planning out the build order: constants/palette/textures, the root and lid joints, dais and posts, chest body, lid, heightfield, coins and gems, crown, goblets, necklace/ring/pouch/crystals, sparkles, then posing the lid and returning the root. Defining the root and lid joints...

Defining gold paint colors...

Still writing velvet quilt pattern...

Positioning the lid's underside plane just slightly below the base plane's surface to avoid z-fighting, since a single-sided plane only renders its front face.

I'm sketching a sparkle SVG as a four-pointed star shape filled white, then thinking about whether to give it a cyan-tinted core to match the glow texture.

Now I'm designing a rune ring SVG with concentric circles, tick marks, and glyph shapes like triangles and chevrons placed around the ring in cyan tones.

Working out the dais geometry, I'm sizing the ground plane and ring to fit the dais apothem, then placing gold hex-column posts at eight vertex positions around the dais perimeter.

Now I'm turning to the chest's wall construction, setting up the outer box bounds, wall thickness, and vertical placement relative to the body's base height.

The mound rises slightly above the rim, about 0.09 over, which looks right. Now I'm positioning the wall boxes around the body, starting with the front wall placed just below the rim using the body's bottom coordinate as reference.

Writing wood plank paint function...

Now thinking about the top rim band—adding gold trim strips around the mouth of the box, four boxes positioned near the top height with slight outward width extension for a decorative lip.

Working out the strip overlaps so the inner edge tucks in about 1.5cm as a rim lip, then mirroring that for the back strip and sizing the side strips to match. I'm applying the same banding logic to the bottom edge now, then moving on to the corner pieces.

Adding corner brackets with iron boxes and gold caps, plus rivets built as merged sphere clusters on the bracket faces and straps. Still writing geometry...

Positioning it at the front so it sticks out slightly toward the viewer, then adding a small cyan gem shape lathed into a diamond facet on top of it.

For the bezel ring I'm using a thin gold torus sized to frame the gem, lying flat so it faces forward naturally without rotation. I'm skipping the keyhole slot idea and instead thinking about whether to add filigree leaf decals around the shield, and now working out where the matching hasp shield sits on the closed lid using the arch's parametric curve near the front edge.

Positioning the hasp tab as a hanging plate proud of the rim strip...

Since the lid rotates open to about 108°, I need to think through which direction the hasp plate extends relative to the lid's rotated frame rather than world space. I'll also add a ruby gem mounted on the hasp, then move on to defining the lid's arch path.

Writing arch sampling math...

Planning gold dome studs along each strap and a front lip bar at the lid edge, plus back hinge barrels and leaf plates split between body and lid. I'll leave the lid tooth alone and move on to interior lining panels in the chest.

I'm placing a red interior lining panel against the back inner wall, positioned just below the rim, then setting up a heightfield grid to shape the terrain-like surface across the chest's footprint.

I need to tune the height formula so flat areas sit just below the dais surface, but I'm noticing the interior dome region creates a steep ramp where it meets the exterior walls—this needs to stay hidden below the rim except where the interior genuinely rises above it.

For coloring, I'll use a flat dark gold like "#b8621a" for the heightfield base, since it's mostly covered by coins and only peeks through gaps. For the geometry itself, I'm building a custom BufferGeometry with positions and indices, computing vertex normals, and skipping UVs since there's no texture to map.

For scattered gems I'll reuse the heap sampler via a `sampleHeap()` helper. For the pearl necklace, I'm planning an irregular closed loop around a lump position using a Catmull-Rom spline, rendered as a thin gold chain tube with pearls as merged spheres placed along the path at sampled points, plus a pendant to anchor it.

Still shaping the pendant placement and defining the leather pouch profile for a lathe shape...

I'm leaning the pouch against the coin heap, tilting it slightly with a few coins poking out of the mouth, settling on a crimson leather color with a gold tie cord, and now I'm adding a gold torus ring nearby.

Positioning a crown region on the left heap peak, computing its height offset and tilt orientation using a quaternion aimed along a lean direction.

For the crown itself, I'm defining the fur trim as a closed circular sweep path near the base using a ring of points swept with a small radius in color F.

Then I'm adding a gold band above the trim using a lathed profile with a flared top, followed by a crimson cap dome lathed from a profile narrowing from the base up to a point near the top.

For the ten crown prongs, I'm alternating tall and short ones at 36-degree intervals, curving each outward from the base in the band to a flaring, dynamic tip near the crown's full height.

Each prong tip gets a small faceted gem, cycling through ruby, sapphire, emerald, and amethyst colors with a cyan one at the front, plus I'm adding ten outward-facing gems set in gold bezels around the band itself.

Now I'm sketching the goblet constructor function that takes placement config and builds the region with position and rotation.

Goblet A is upright gold with cyan liquid: the body uses a lathe profile painted gold with smoothing disabled to avoid corner-crossing at the thin lip, a brighter gold ring swept around the rim, and the liquid rendered as a short cyan cylinder sitting inside.

Still positioning glow and meniscus...

I'm adding six small gems around the bowl's waist, a gold collar band where the bowl meets the stem, a flattened stem knob, and a filigree decal placed on the front of the bowl.

Now I'm sizing the goblet's bowl radius and overall height for a chunky look, then working out how a second, tipped-over goblet should rest on its side -- figuring out the axis tilt so it leans against its rim and foot edge convincingly.

Goblet B's foot sits at one point and the mouth tilts down roughly 10°, resting against the surface; I'm computing the position by placing the foot center offset from a midpoint along the tilted axis, then deriving the orientation quaternion from that axis direction. Now I'm planning goblet C as a taller, slender chalice with a narrower V-shaped bowl, emerald accents, and a swirled stem for visual variety.

I'm sketching a parametrized goblet function that takes a region, scale, body color, trim color, gem color, and optional liquid color, applying the scale manually inside the outline coordinates since the lathe geometry uses literal values rather than region-based scaling. I'm defining the outline function for the cup and chalice profiles now.

Still writing outline coordinates...

For the liquid surface, I'm setting it near the lip with a radius slightly under the inner wall. The tipped goblet skips liquid entirely and instead shows spilled coins and gems scattered at the mouth. I'm sketching a filigree decal texture with scroll-wave paths and diamond accents in dark orange, scaled appropriately for a 512px canvas, and starting on crystal cluster shapes next.

Now I'm setting up the coin color palette — gold, silver, and bronze rims with matching face tints — and planning arrays to batch coin geometries by type so they can be merged efficiently, writing a helper function to add each coin's cylinder and face geometry into those arrays.

With the geometry collections planned, I'm turning to the random sampling functions needed for scattering treasure across the heap — a seeded RNG, a Gaussian sampler for natural clustering, and a weighted spot picker that favors bumps based on their size.

I still need to work out keepout zones so coins don't spawn inside the chest, under the crown, or under goblet feet, and I'm starting to pin down exact coordinates for each major object like the crown and the upright goblet.

Now I'm placing the remaining pieces: the second upright goblet on one heap, the tipped goblet with its foot and mouth position so spilled coins trail from it naturally, and scattering a few hero gems like a ruby and sapphire along with a coin pouch near the dais edge.

I'm also positioning the necklace draped over a lump, a ring lying flat near a gem, several coin stacks of varying heights scattered across the dais, and two crystal clusters (cyan and amethyst) placed toward the back corners for visual balance.

Setting up imports for the builder, path, paint, and texture modules, then starting on the scene metadata.

Writing the placement helper...

Defining the dais lathe outline...

I'll add a glowing rune plane positioned under the heightfield, scatter loose coins across the dais floor over the rune ring, and set up sparkle card frames with flickering flow for the particle effects.

Finishing up the gem color palette with sapphire, amethyst, cyan, and pink, then setting up a helper function to add gems with position, direction, size, and spin, grouping them by color so matching gems merge into shared geometry. I'm also bundling all the gold accent pieces—rivets, studs, bezels—into a single flat-colored merged geometry for the crown's metal bits.

Now I'm sketching out the chest's corner feet as chunky iron-painted boxes, then setting up an arch helper function that computes 3D points along an elliptical curve using the ellipse's normal vector for lift offset—mapping the ellipse's u/v coordinates into the scene's z/y axes. I'm verifying the normal vector derivation is correct before moving on to defining the lid's side-view outline.

Writing lid geometry...

Resolving the lit paint using position and normal without an explicit surface falls back to the current surface context, which works since the outer scope sets it, and when lit itself is an unresolved Paint object it's returned directly as allowed. Now I'm moving on to defining the body wall paint.

For the dais I'm using a stone-textured scale paint with a derived shadow color, which should resolve fine since cel's shadow comes from the resolved base paint. I also need to build a rune ring SVG generator and double-check the Region API signature by looking at src/region.ts.

input.command: sed -n 1,80p src/region.ts; ls samples scratch 2>/dev/null | head; cat package.json | head -30
